articles.headline: The Little Missouri Stockmen's Association.
articles.text:
Minutes of the meeting of the stockmen of the Little Missouri, held at Medora, Dakota, December 19, 1884:

The following companies and individuals were represented:

SOHO Cattle Company.
Badger Cattle Company.
Custer Trail Cattle Company.
Le Moyne Cattle Company.
Maltese Cross Cattle Company.
Elkhorn Cattle Company.
Thompson & Co.
L. D. & B. Rumsey.
H. B. Wadsworth & Co.
N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.
Casey & Co.

The meeting was called to order by Theodore Roosevelt.

The following resolution was read and adopted;

RESOLVED, That it is the sense of the stockmen present, representing the companies and individuals named above, that an association of the stockmen of the Little Missouri and its tributaries be forthwith formed, and that this association shall be known as The Little Missouri Stockmen's Association.

Also the following:

The officers of the association shall consist of a chairman and vice-chairman, elected annually, at the first meeting held after the fall round-up, and a secretary elected at each meeting, whose work is to be superintended by the chairman.

Theodore Roosevelt was elected chair-main, and Henry S. Boice vice-chairman.

The Marquis de Mores was nominated as a committee of one to work with the committee appointed by the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association in the endeavor to procure legislation from the territorial legislature of Dakota favorable to the interest of cattle men.

A resolution was passed that if any of the members of the association had cattle run over by the railroad, for which cattle the railroad refused to pay full value, it should be at once brought to the notice of the chairman, who shall report it to the next meeting of the association, in order that it might be brought before the courts as a test case.

The following resolutions were also passed:

RESOLVED, That at the request, in writing, of any three members of the association, a meeting shall be called by the chairman, who shall, however, give at least one weeks notice thereof.

RESOLVED, That the representation in this association be by firm, each firm being entitled to but one vote.

RESOLVED, That the next meeting of the association be held on or about April 1, 1885, at the call of the convention.

RESOLVED, That if any of the cattle companies or stockmen along the river refuse to conform to the rules and by-laws of this association, that it will refuse to act with them or allow them to take part in the round-up; and the captain of the round-up shall see that no stockman debarred by action of this association from participating in the round-up is allowed to take part in it and he shall further see that no third party, acting in the interest of said stockman is permitted to take part in or derive benefit from the round-up.

RESOLVED, That no member shall gather cattle or brand calves between December 1 and the date of the general spring round-up, without giving due notice a reasonable time beforehand to the other ranchmen of the neighborhood.

RESOLVED, That each member shall hereafter have not less than 10 bulls to every 100 head of stock on his range.

RESOLVED, That the chairman draw up a series of by-laws for the association, or embodying the foregoing resolutions and in other respects following, so far as they are practicable, the laws of the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association.

At 1:10 p. m. the meeting adjourned.
articles.summary: Minutes of the December 19, 1884 Medora meeting that formed the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association, with Theodore Roosevelt elected chairman, Henry S. Boice vice-chairman, and the Marquis de Mores named to work with the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association on territorial legislation.

articles.text: The stockmen's meeting last Friday morning bids fair to be the beginning of a very efficient organization. The utmost harmony and unanimity prevailed, and under the able chairmanship of Theodore Roosevelt, a large amount of business was transacted in a short time. It is of especial interest to every stockman on the river to carefully read the minutes of the meeting and act accordingly. Every motion that was passed was carefully discussed, and when it was seen to be for the greatest good of the greatest number, was unanimously declared the sense of the meeting. Especial provision was made for the fact that the large companies would be apt to have things too much their way, by allowing each company to have but one vote. The intention of the organization is not to be an independent concern, run on an expensive scale. It is more on the mutual benefit plan, and will probably be made subordinate to the Eastern Montana Association. A first-rate start was made, and we can now look forward to an efficient organization ruling all stock matters on the river. May success attend "The Little Missouri Stockmen's Association."
articles.summary: Packard praises the stockmen's meeting and Roosevelt's able chairmanship, noting one vote per company and likely subordination to the Eastern Montana Association.

articles.text: Basing conclusions upon the fact that buffalo are almost extinct, many papers are foretelling the fact that deer in this part of the country will all soon be killed, and are calling for a law restricting the time of killing. It is an understood fact that their numbers will diminish, but our children's children will still be killing them. There is scarcely a state in the Union in which deer are not found, and long after their extinction elsewhere, the natural hiding places of the Bad Lands will give them shelter. There are a large number of persons who make their living killing deer, and it is doubted by those who should know if the total number of deer in the Bad Lands has materially decreased. We are no advocate of the wholesale slaughter of venison, but we will never see the deer exterminated from this country, and as the few that are killed are used for food and not for the sole pleasure of killing, we even think the game law should be extended another month instead of being decreased.
articles.summary: Editorial arguing Bad Lands deer will not be exterminated and that the game law season should be extended rather than shortened.

articles.text: An item has been going the rounds of newspapers as follows: "There is too much money invested in cattle in the United States for our friends to allow temporary differences of opinion to last. Two and a half billions of dollars is the size of that investment. There has been much good work accomplished, and there remains much to be done. With everybody in the harness and all the collars pressing evenly on the shoulders the work will be easily done." The report of the commissioner of agriculture for January, 1883, gives the total number of cattle in the United States as 41,172,762, valued at $1,008,124, 516. The paragrapher who originated the item only missed the valuation $1,491,875,484; but a billion, several million, and a few hundred thousand dollars cut no figure in an average editor's calculations. However, this bull writer ought to put the "collars" on his head until it could be reduced to commonplace consideration.
articles.summary: Packard corrects a widely copied item on the value of U.S. cattle using the commissioner of agriculture's January 1883 figures.

articles.text: A stock owner went out the other day over the divide to see how his cattle were standing the vigorous weather, and found a large fine steer in his last long sleep. The stockmen had to roll him over to see the brand, and he has regretted his curiosity ever since. He told me that the brand looked to him like a Roman candle making about a thousand revolutions per minute, and with 187 more prismatic colors than he thought were in existence. Sometimes a steer is not dead, but is in a cold stupor which precedes death, and when stirred up a little and irritated because he cannot die without turning over and showing his brand, he musters his remaining strength and kicks the inquisitive stockman so high that he can see and recognize the features of departed friends. That was the way it happened on this occasion. The stockmen fell in the branches of a pine on Jack creek, not dead, but very thoughtful.—[Laramie Boomerang.
articles.summary: Humorous clipping from the Laramie Boomerang about a stockman kicked by a freezing steer.

articles.text: The ball to-night at Roberts & Co.'s hall, bids fair to outdo anything we have had yet in the terpsichorean line. Certain it is that no pains or expense was spared in getting out the programmes, and the COW BOY is proud of them as the neatest specimen of job work we have yet turned out. Everyone should attend the dance and secure a programme as a trophy.

articles.text: Joe McCool had a streak of luck last week that is rarely duplicated. A bronco was put up for raffle with ten chances. Joe won. The next day he won a Remington rifle under the same conditions. The next day he put up his bronco, kept a chance, and won again. Total outlay, $10; total receipts, a bronco, a rifle and $45 cash. The chances were one in ten, which he accepted and won three times in succession.
articles.summary: Joe McCool won three ten-chance raffles in succession.

articles.text: A great excitement has been raised in eastern and southern Dakota over the fact that coal has been discovered there. The St. Paul Globe speaks about the report of a three-foot vein being found, but says it lacks confirmation. From the coal veins in the Bad Lands, there seems to be little doubt that the whole of Dakota, or the greater part of it, is underlaid with vast beds of coal. In the Bad Lands themselves five veins are sometimes seen in one butte, the veins running from three to nine and twelve feet. There is a vein between Ferris Bros. & Merrifield's and Lloyd Roberts' ranches which is twenty feet thick in sight. It runs down to the surface of the river, and may extend twenty feet more from that point as far as any one knows. Forty-five miles south of here, at Mattox' ranch, on the old tie trail, there is a vein forty feet thick in plain sight on apparently the same level as the one spoken of above. At Buffalo creek, fifty miles from here on the stage road, in the midst of the prairie, a good vein has been found on the surface and another at a depth of forty-two feet. Between South Moreau and Indian Creek, a hundred and forty miles south of here, a vein was discovered at a depth of seventy-eight feet. It seems almost impossible to sink a well any distance anywhere in Dakota without passing through one or more veins of coal. There is enough coal in the Bad Lands to supply the universe for ages, but we might casually remark that as far as it is concerned, the universe will remain unsupplied as long as the prohibitive charges of the Northern Pacific remain in force.
articles.summary: Editorial on Dakota coal: veins throughout the Bad Lands, but Northern Pacific rates keep it from market.
